---
title: Getting started
---

alpha-led-sign controls Alpha-protocol LED message signs over a serial line. It was
built for, and tested on, an Alpha 4120C. It has profiles for the rest of the 4000
Series and the BetaBrite, and a generic profile for any Alpha sign.

## Install

alpha-led-sign needs Python 3.12 or later. Its only dependency is
[pyserial](https://pyserial.readthedocs.io/). Install it from
[PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/alpha-led-sign/):

```sh
uv add alpha-led-sign
# or
pip install alpha-led-sign
```

The `cli` extra adds the [`alpha-led-sign` command](11-command-line.qmd):
`pip install 'alpha-led-sign[cli]'`.

The import name is `alpha_led_sign`, distinct from the older `alphasign`
library.

## Connect a Sign

A 4000 Series Sign has an RJ11 serial port. Connect it to a USB serial adapter,
then open the Sign by the adapter's device name:

```python
from alpha_led_sign import Sign, models

with Sign.serial("/dev/ttyUSB0", model=models.ALPHA_4120C) as sign:
    sign.show("Hello")
```

On macOS the device is named like `/dev/tty.usbserial-1410`; on Windows it is a
`COM` port. The `with` block closes the port at the end.

`show` writes TEXT File `A`, which every Sign has when it powers up, so this works
on a Sign fresh from the box. The display goes blank for a moment while the File is
written.

### Line settings

The defaults are 9600 baud, 8 data bits, no parity, and 1 stop bit. Alpha 1.0 Signs
also accept 7 data bits, even parity, and 2 stop bits, at 1200 to 9600 baud:

```python
from alpha_led_sign import SerialFormat

sign = Sign.serial(
    "/dev/ttyUSB0", baudrate=4800, serial_format=SerialFormat.SEVEN_E_TWO
)
```

`Sign.serial` takes any [pyserial URL](https://pyserial.readthedocs.io/en/latest/url_handlers.html),
so `socket://host:port` reaches a Sign through a serial-to-TCP bridge. The bridge
must keep the short silences the protocol needs: some Commands need the line quiet
for 100 ms at a fixed point. A bridge that merges writes can remove those pauses.

## Choose a Sign Model and Sign Address

The `model` tells the library two things: which Sign Type to address, and what the
Sign can show. With `models.ALPHA_4120C`, the library addresses 4120C Signs and
warns before it sends a Mode or color a 4120C does not have. See
[Sign Models and validation](08-sign-models.qmd).

Without a `model`, the library uses `models.GENERIC`. It addresses every Alpha Sign
and checks only the Protocol Version.

The `address` picks one Sign among Signs of the same Sign Type on one line. The
default, 0, is the broadcast address: every matching Sign acts on what you send.
That is fine for writes to a single Sign. Reads need the Sign's own address,
because every Sign that matches answers and their answers collide:

```python
with Sign.serial("/dev/ttyUSB0", model=models.ALPHA_4120C, address=1) as sign:
    print(sign.info())
```

[Reading back and discovery](07-reading-and-discovery.qmd) shows how to find the
addresses of the Signs on a line.

## Try it without a Sign

The repository has an emulator in `emulator/`: a program that acts like one or
more Signs and draws what each one shows in a web page. It needs Node. From a
clone of the repository:

```sh
cd emulator
npm ci
npm run serve
```

Then open it as a serial port at `socket://127.0.0.1:4120`:

```python
with Sign.serial("socket://127.0.0.1:4120", model=models.ALPHA_4120C) as sign:
    sign.show("{color green}It works")
```

The emulator follows the manual, not the firmware. Content that looks right there
can still look different on a real Sign.
